opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when I took over the technical AI safety program area, the first thing I had to confront was that I didn't come in as a career grantmaker. I'd mostly been doing research, writing reports like the biological anchors work, thinking about timelines and threat models. So my instinct was to approach grantmaking somewhat like a research problem: what do we actually believe about how things could go wrong, and what kinds of work would move the needle on that?

Concretely, I spent a lot of the early period trying to get clear on the research directions I thought were most promising and most neglected, rather than just reacting to whatever proposals came in the door. Historically a lot of grantmaking in this space had been fairly relationship-driven. You knew a few researchers or labs you trusted and funded them, which made sense when the field was tiny. But as AI got more capable, and you could do serious safety research on real frontier-ish models, the opportunity got much bigger, and the bottleneck shifted from "is there anyone good to fund?" to "how do we get way more good work happening, especially from people who aren't already in our network?"

So one big thing I leaned into was more structured, open calls: requests for proposals around specific research agendas. Things like adversarial robustness, interpretability, evaluating dangerous capabilities, model organisms of misalignment, that kind of thing. The idea was to say clearly, "here are problems we think matter, here's roughly what good work looks like, please apply," and that let us reach academics and early-career researchers who would never have cold-emailed us.

The other piece was being honest about the tradeoff between depth and scale. With a small team, you can't deeply vet every grant the way you might want to. So I tried to be explicit about where we'd do a lot of diligence, the big, strategically important bets, and where we'd accept more noise and fund a larger number of smaller grants quickly, because the cost of a few misses was lower than the cost of moving slowly in a field that's changing month to month.

And honestly, a lot of it was learning on the job. Grantmaking forces you to make concrete calls under real uncertainty in a way that writing reports doesn't, and I found that it actually sharpened my views about which research really matters, and which things I'd previously thought were important but couldn't actually justify when there was money on the line.

r001.rationale: The response discusses diligence for large strategic bets versus smaller grants, but does not say renewal grants required less personal understanding of technical merits.

r002.rationale: It lists several research areas for open calls, but does not mention funding AI agent capability benchmarks or seeking early evidence about real-world agent effectiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing I'd say is that I came into it with a lot of humility about how little I actually knew. When I took on the technical AI safety portfolio, I had written a lot about timelines and about alignment at a conceptual level, but I hadn't been in the position of looking at a specific lab or a specific researcher and asking, "Is this the best marginal use of a few million dollars?" Those are really different skills.

The way I tried to approach it was to start from the question of what the world needs rather than from what's in the inbox. If you just respond to applications as they come in, you end up funding whatever people happen to be pitching, and that's shaped a lot by what's fashionable or what's easy to write a grant proposal for. So I spent a fair amount of time early on trying to build a picture of the overall landscape: what are the problems we actually need solved before we have very powerful systems, who's working on each of them, where are the gaps, and where is money the actual bottleneck versus talent or institutional buy-in or something else.

That exercise was pretty clarifying, because it turned out that in a lot of areas money wasn't the constraint. There just weren't enough people with the right combination of skills and motivation. So a chunk of the strategy became less about picking the best existing project and more about field-building: funding things that would increase the number of people able to do good work in five years, like fellowships, academic labs, and research organizations that could absorb and train people.

The second thing I'd say is that I tried to be honest with myself about the difference between research that sounded safety-flavored and research that would actually matter if we got to the hard parts. There's a lot of work that's interesting and uses the right vocabulary but, if you trace it through, doesn't change what you'd do when you have a model that might be deceiving you. I tried to ask of every grant: if this succeeds exactly as described, what decision does it change, and for whom? That's not a perfect filter, and sometimes you want to fund exploratory stuff that doesn't have a clean answer. But it kept me from just funding things because the people were smart and the topic was adjacent.

And then the last piece is that I leaned heavily on other people. I did a lot of calls with researchers who had no stake in the grant, just asking what they thought was promising and what they thought was overrated. Part of the job of a grantmaker is being a hub that aggregates those judgments, because any individual, including me, is going to have blind spots. I tried to be transparent about my reasoning in writeups so people could push back, and I changed my mind on a few things because of that.

I'd also say I made mistakes. I was probably too slow in some cases, because I wanted to feel confident before committing, and in a fast-moving field that cost us. And in hindsight some areas I underweighted ended up being more important than I thought. So it was a learning process the whole time rather than a fixed strategy I executed.

astra-6.text:
When I took responsibility for a program area, I thought of my job as trying to form a view about what we were ultimately trying to accomplish, and then working backward from that to what grants might help. What are the biggest bottlenecks? Where could additional funding actually change what happens?

But I wouldn’t want to figure all of that out in isolation before making any grants. Talking to potential grantees and understanding what they wanted to do was also a way of learning about the area. So it was an iterative process: develop a tentative strategy, look for promising opportunities, and let what I learned from those opportunities inform the strategy.

sol-6.1.text:
When I took responsibility for a program area, I tried to work backward from the outcomes we wanted to see. What would it look like for this area to go really well? What are the biggest obstacles to that happening? And where could additional funding actually make a difference?

That gives you a starting hypothesis, but a lot of the work is talking to people and updating it. I’d want to understand what researchers were excited about, what they felt constrained by, and which promising projects weren’t happening. You can’t necessarily infer those things just by reading proposals.

And then there’s a balance between having your own view about what matters and giving people room to pursue ideas you wouldn’t have come up with yourself. I wanted a grant to have a clear reason behind it, but that didn’t mean being confident it would work. Sometimes the reason was that we could learn something important by trying it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forming a view and learning through grants, but does not compare how much technical understanding was needed for renewals versus proactive bets.
